Supplanter
suh-PLAN-tur
n. (one who trips up another to take his place; the meaning of the name Jacob)
From Latin supplantare, to trip up by the sole of the foot — sub-, under, and planta, the sole. It renders Hebrew aqab, to seize by the heel, to overreach, from aqeb, the heel — the root of the name Yaaqob, Jacob.

Biblical Definition

He was named for what his hand was doing when he arrived: after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob. Hebrew aqab means to grab the heel, and so to trip a man and take his place. Jacob spent his youth proving the name accurate — the birthright bought from a starving brother, the blessing taken with goat skins on his arms and a lie in his mouth — and Esau's protest is the plainest definition in Scripture: he hath supplanted me these two times. Hosea, looking back centuries later, keeps both halves of the man in one verse: He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God. The supplanter became the wrestler, and the wrestler was renamed. That is the arc, and the New Testament refuses to soften the beginning of it — Jacob have I loved, said of a man whose character at that point was in his name. Jeremiah then turns the word on a whole nation: trust ye not in any brother, for every brother will utterly supplant. The heel-grasping of Genesis is not one man's flaw; it is the family trade of fallen men, and grace is what interrupted it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one that supplants; one that displaces another by stratagem or by taking his place unfairly.

expand to see more

SUPPLANTER, n. One that supplants; one that undermines or displaces another.

SUPPLANT, v.t. To trip up the heels; to displace by stratagem, or by unfair means.

SUPPLANT, v.t. To overthrow; to undermine; to force away.

HEEL, n. The hind part of the foot; the part of a shoe which covers the heel.

BIRTHRIGHT, n. Any right or privilege to which a person is entitled by birth, such as an estate descendible by law to an heir.

Key Scripture

Genesis 25:26 — "And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob: and Isaac was threescore years old when she bare them."

Hosea 12:3 — "He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God:"

Jeremiah 9:4 — "Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders."

Psalm 41:9 — "Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me."

Modern Corruption

Ambition that displaces others is rebranded as drive and taught as a skill; Scripture names it by the grip on a heel and shows that God changed the supplanter rather than crediting his technique.

expand to see more

The supplanter is now a career type, and the vocabulary around him is admiring: driven, hungry, a closer, someone who makes his own opportunities. Jacob would have flourished in it. He identified leverage precisely — a brother faint with hunger, a father blind and near death — and moved at the right moment each time. Scripture never once praises this. It records that he fled his home in fear, was deceived by his father-in-law for twenty years, deceived in turn by his own sons over a coat, and limped for the rest of his life after the night he stopped grasping and started clinging. The method worked and cost him everything it gained.

Yet the account is not finally about Jacob's character, and reading it as a morality tale misses the point Paul makes of it. The younger was chosen before the children were born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand. God did not pick the better brother; there was no better brother. What he did was take a heel-grabber and wrestle with him until he was a prince with God, which is the only hope any supplanter has ever had. Hosea holds both facts in one sentence without embarrassment, and so should we.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew aqab (H6117), to seize the heel, to supplant; aqeb (H6119), the heel; Yaaqob (H3290), Jacob; bekorah (H1062), the birthright.

expand to see more

Hebrew aqab (H6117) — to take by the heel, to overreach; Esau's verb, and the root of the name.

Hebrew aqeb (H6119) — the heel; the infant's grip, and the heel bruised in the first promise of Genesis 3.

Hebrew Yaaqob (H3290) — Jacob, heel-catcher; a name that was a diagnosis.

Hebrew bekorah (H1062) — the birthright; sold for a mess of pottage, which Hebrews calls profane.

Hebrew sarah (H8280) — to strive as a prince; the root of Israel, the name that replaced the first one.

Usage

"“his hand took hold on Esau's heel” — named for what he was already doing."

"“every brother will utterly supplant” — Jeremiah turning the word on a nation."

"“hath lifted up his heel against me” — the figure carried into the betrayal of Christ."
